video_title: Jake Paul & The Chainsmokers: Turning Fame into Funds, Jake Enters Politics? & Venture Bubble Signs
gist: All-In summit segments: Jake Paul on turning attention into a UFC rival (MVP/PFL) and a $100M 'Anti Fund', then the Chainsmokers on running a Series A venture fund, with warnings of venture bubble signs such as 2-3x markups on second tranches.

insights.claim: Jake Paul's venture fund argues that capital is a commodity and attention is the scarce input, so it sells distribution, branding and cap-table visibility to founders as its differentiator.
insights.speaker: Jake Paul
insights.so_what: Celebrity-led funds are pricing attention as an edge over plain capital; test whether it shows up in DPI.
insights.quote: we're in the attention economy and that capital um is a commodity

insights.claim: Paul cites Elon Musk's Twitter ownership, where the first suggested follow for new accounts is Musk, as a mechanism for promoting all of his companies.
insights.speaker: Jake Paul
insights.so_what: Platform ownership is itself a distribution subsidy for portfolio companies.

insights.claim: Paul says he told OpenAI to launch a social media app, was involved in building the Sora app, and granted his name, image and likeness (NIL) so users can make videos with it.
insights.speaker: Jake Paul
insights.so_what: Sora's launch used creator NIL licensing as a seeding tactic; creator-licensed generative video is a pattern to watch.

insights.claim: Paul warns the attention economy's downside is inauthenticity: people build things to gain eyeballs rather than build great things, and outrage hot takes in journalism and content are made because they earn views and money.
insights.speaker: Jake Paul
insights.so_what: Incentives reward engagement over substance, which is a quality discount risk for attention-driven businesses.

insights.claim: Paul argues no single platform will curb clickbait because a platform that restricts content loses viewership to Twitch, Kick, Twitter, Instagram or TikTok, a race-to-the-bottom he compares to the US-Russia-China AI race.
insights.speaker: Jake Paul
insights.so_what: Platform self-regulation is a collective-action problem, so content-moderation costs are unlikely to rise voluntarily.

themes.theme: Jake Paul's MVP/PFL challenge to the UFC

insights.claim: Paul claims the UFC pays fighters roughly 15% of revenue versus about 50% in other pro leagues, and says this creates fighter discontent and talent leakage to boxing that his promotion can exploit.
insights.speaker: Jake Paul
insights.so_what: A margin-gap pitch: Paul's challenge is to attract talent by revenue share; watch UFC talent retention and fighter-pay terms.
insights.quote: they pay their fighters roughly 15% of their total revenue

insights.claim: Paul says his promotion MVP now has about 400 boxing and MMA fighters, has merged with PFL, and aims to be the Pepsi or Adidas to the UFC's Coke or Nike.
insights.speaker: Jake Paul
insights.so_what: The first credible UFC competitor is being assembled by merger; scale and distribution deals are the tests.

insights.claim: Paul's boxing model replicates his Team 10 influencer-incubator: he uses a 100 million-follower built-in audience to promote fighters from the start, instead of the traditional slow build of an unbeaten record.
insights.speaker: Jake Paul
insights.so_what: Owned audience lets a promoter bypass traditional record-building and monetize fighters earlier.

insights.claim: Paul says his Tyson fight on Netflix drew 138 million viewers, which he treated as evidence of boxing's pay-per-view potential.
insights.speaker: Jake Paul
insights.so_what: Streaming platforms are bidding for live-event audiences at very large scale.

insights.claim: Paul says Vine's top 20 creators demanded a million dollars each per year, Twitter offered a pooled million, and the creators left for Facebook, YouTube and Snapchat, after which Vine died within months.
insights.speaker: Jake Paul
insights.so_what: Platforms that underpay the creators who supply their traffic risk collapse when the creators leave.

insights.claim: Paul's Anti Fund raised $100 million, is now on fund four, and runs a barbell strategy of first checks in early founders plus growth-stage bets on top founders like Sam and Palmer; he wants to be judged on DPI and IRR against Sequoia.
insights.speaker: Jake Paul
insights.so_what: Fund-level DPI and IRR will be the real test of the celebrity-VC model.
insights.quote: compare me to the Sequoas of the world, our DPI and IRR

insights.claim: Paul says he is an investor in OpenAI, Cognition and SpaceX through his fund.
insights.speaker: Jake Paul
insights.so_what: Celebrity funds are accessing late-stage AI and space names, likely via SPVs or secondaries.

insights.claim: A Chainsmokers co-founder says their fund invests at Series A, does not take lead positions, focuses on cybersecurity, AI infrastructure, deep tech and health tech, and uses brand and go-to-market access as value-add.
insights.speaker: Chainsmokers co-founder (Drew/Alex)
insights.so_what: Non-lead, value-add seed and Series A funds differentiate on distribution rather than on price.

insights.claim: A Chainsmokers co-founder says the fund's value proposition is brand building as AI makes tech products indefensible, so companies need to 'suck the oxygen out of the room'.
insights.speaker: Chainsmokers co-founder (Drew/Alex)
insights.so_what: If AI erodes product moats, brand and distribution become the more durable moat.
insights.quote: the defensibil indefensibility that AI has created around tech

insights.claim: A Chainsmokers co-founder says their fund recently had one of its first proper liquidity events, with fund-one company Underdog Fantasy sold to HG IG International, and that they are letting winners such as Dandy ride because it keeps doubling every year.
insights.speaker: Chainsmokers co-founder (Drew/Alex)
insights.so_what: Young funds are only now returning DPI from 2019-vintage investments.

themes.theme: Venture bubble signs and fund structure

insights.claim: A Chainsmokers co-founder says double and triple tranche deals now see the second-tranche buyer pay two to three times the initial valuation with no change in underlying performance; Jason Calacanis calls it bubble behavior.
insights.speaker: Chainsmokers co-founder (Drew/Alex)
insights.so_what: Markups with no fundamental change are a classic late-cycle signal in private markets.
insights.quote: paying a significant markup sometimes two or three what the company is initially valued at for absolutely no change in underlying performance

insights.claim: A Chainsmokers co-founder says so much liquidity is flowing into venture that companies get marked up just because of the people involved, and that they avoid hyped companies they see as sure markups but lacking long-term vision.
insights.speaker: Chainsmokers co-founder (Drew/Alex)
insights.so_what: Abundant liquidity lets weak companies get marked up, so mark-to-model returns may overstate quality.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis argues unicorns should be redefined by a billion dollars in revenue rather than valuation, and says one of his companies has just hit $700 million in revenue.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Revenue-based thresholds are a cleaner filter than paper valuations in an inflated market.

insights.claim: Calacanis says funds can now run early and late-stage businesses side by side because companies stay private longer; SPVs let family offices buy late stage while early investors sell, with Sequoia and Founders Fund both buying and selling in Stripe and SpaceX.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Secondary and SPV liquidity is becoming a core business line for venture firms.

insights.claim: A Chainsmokers co-founder notes that Founders Fund forces itself to put 25% of each fund's capital into one winner, and that concentrating in winners is a skill that takes time to learn.
insights.speaker: Chainsmokers co-founder (Drew/Alex)
insights.so_what: Forced concentration policy is a structural way to capture power-law returns.

insights.claim: A Chainsmokers co-founder says venture returns are power-law, with the top 5% of companies generating about 90% of returns, and that venture is the last frontier for celebrity investors because assets are long-duration and illiquid.
insights.speaker: Chainsmokers co-founder (Drew/Alex)
insights.so_what: Returns are concentrated, so access to the best companies matters more than breadth.

insights.claim: Calacanis says 19 of 21 angels he introduced to Travis Kalanick declined to back Uber because it was a 'dirty' real-world business and they wanted software only, while Robin Hood was likewise laughed at early.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Non-obvious, operationally messy businesses are often overlooked by software-only investors.

insights.claim: An investor at the summit says he passed on Robin Hood because his prior experience building Facebook's growth mechanism violated his priors, calling it a billion dollar mistake, and warns that past losses or wins in a sector bias judgment.
insights.speaker: Panelist (investor)
insights.so_what: Prior experience can be a blind spot; ask 'what if this works?' before dismissing.

insights.claim: Calacanis observes that many great investors had no prior experience in their asset class, such as Mike Morris as a journalist and John Doerr as an Intel chip salesman.
insights.speaker: Panelist
insights.so_what: Outsider perspective may help avoid priors, though the claim is unverified.

insights.claim: A Chainsmokers co-founder says the ability to generate consistent DPI cuts through all noise because investors have short memories for anything other than returns, so converting fame or attention into results is the only durable credential.
insights.speaker: Chainsmokers co-founder (Drew/Alex)
insights.so_what: LPs back fame-led funds only after realized returns.

insights.claim: The Chainsmokers say about 300,000 songs are now uploaded to Spotify every day, and if they started over today they would not know how to break through.
insights.speaker: Chainsmokers co-founder (Drew/Alex)
insights.so_what: Supply glut makes discovery the bottleneck, so owned audience and live events dominate.
insights.quote: 300,000 songs being uploaded to Spotify every day

insights.claim: The Chainsmokers say they are interested in who will be the first new artist to reject the label model and go direct to fans, and argue AI, streaming and YouTube make the music business unpredictable.
insights.speaker: Chainsmokers co-founder (Drew/Alex)
insights.so_what: The label model faces disintermediation as distribution and community tools get cheaper.

insights.claim: The Chainsmokers say live performance as DJs has far better economics than arena tours with a full band, and say they have had a Las Vegas residency for eight years at 'the win'.
insights.speaker: Chainsmokers co-founder (Drew/Alex)
insights.so_what: Live DJ residencies are a high-margin, low-overhead revenue stream versus band touring.

insights.claim: The Chainsmokers say there is a broad nostalgia trend, and Jason Calacanis notes his teenage children's playlists are full of throwback artists like Elton John.
insights.speaker: Chainsmokers co-founder (Drew/Alex)
insights.so_what: Catalog and nostalgia demand is a tailwind for legacy artists and catalog assets.
